subjective.question: What is antiperistalsis?
subjective.answer: The reverse peristalsis is called antiperistalsis, which occurs occasionally. These movements cause the passage of food from the intestine back into the stomach or even into the mouth. This is also called vomiting.

subjective.question: How do fishes live in extremely cold water?
subjective.answer: 1. They have "antifreeze" materials in their blood in the form of polyalcohols (e.g., sorbitol, glycerol) or water-soluble peptides and glycopeptides, because these substances lower the freezing point of blood plasma and other body fluids. 2. These fishes also have proteins or protein-sugar compounds that inhibit the growth of ice crystals that begin to form. 3. These adaptations enable these fishes to stay flexible and swim freely in a super-cooled state (i.e., at a temperature below the normal freezing temperature of the surrounding water).

subjective.question: Define digestion.
subjective.answer: Digestion is the chemical and/or mechanical breakdown of complex food into diffusible molecules, i.e., particles that individual cells of an animal can absorb: starch into glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

subjective.question: Differentiate between intracellular and extracellular digestion.
subjective.answer: Digestion is of two main types: intracellular and extracellular. In intracellular digestion, breakdown of food occurs within the cells: food is first taken into the cell vacuole, the cytoplasm secretes digestive enzymes into the food vacuole, and the enzymes break larger molecules into smaller ones, which enter the cytoplasm. In extracellular digestion, the enzymes are secreted outside the cell into the gut cavity or lumen, where digestion occurs.

subjective.question: Describe the structure of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
subjective.answer: As with any organ, the function of the gastrointestinal tract is determined by the type of tissues it contains. Most of the mammalian gastrointestinal tract has the same anatomical structure along its entire length. From the outside inward is a thin layer of connective tissue called the serosa; the serosa forms a moist epithelial sheet called the peritoneum, which lines the entire abdominal cavity and covers all internal organs. Next are the longitudinal smooth-muscle layer and the circular smooth-muscle layer. Underneath this muscle layer is the submucosa, which contains connective tissue, blood and lymphatic vessels. The mucosa faces the central opening, which is called the lumen. The coordinated contractions of the muscle layers of the gastrointestinal tract mix the food material with various secretions and move the food from the oral cavity to the rectum; the two types of movement involved are peristalsis and segmentation.

subjective.question: Describe digestion in the grasshopper.
subjective.answer: During feeding, the grasshopper's mandibles and maxillae first break up (masticate) the food, which is then taken into the mouth and passed to the crop via the esophagus. The salivary glands secrete saliva, which also contains the enzyme amylase that digests carbohydrates; this digestion continues during food storage in the crop. The midgut secretes other enzymes (carbohydrases, lipases, proteases) that enter the crop. Food passes slowly from the crop to the stomach, where it is mechanically reduced and the nutrient particles sorted. The small particles enter the gastric caeca, where extracellular digestion and absorption is completed. Undigested food is moved along the intestine and passes into the rectum, where water and ions are absorbed. The solid fecal pellets are removed via the anus.

subjective.question: What is the ruminant stomach? How does it help in cellulose digestion?
subjective.answer: Ruminant mammals are the animals that "chew their cud", such as cows, sheep, and deer. The ruminant stomach provides an opportunity for large numbers of microorganisms to digest the cellulose walls of grass and other vegetation. Cellulose contains a large amount of energy; however, animals generally lack the ability to produce the enzyme cellulase for digesting cellulose and obtaining its energy. Because gut microorganisms can produce cellulase, they have made the herbivorous lifestyle more effective.

subjective.question: Define osmoregulation.
subjective.answer: Osmoregulation is defined as the maintenance of constant osmotic pressure in the fluids of an organism by the control of water and salt concentrations. It means osmoregulation governs water and salt balance, and excretion of metabolic wastes. In fishes, reptiles, birds, and mammals, the kidneys are the primary osmoregulatory structure.

subjective.question: How does the primitive streak develop in birds?
subjective.answer: The formation of the primitive streak in the blastocyst involves the coordinated movement and re-arrangement of cells in the epiblast. Even before the streak is visible, epiblast cells have started to move. Two counter-rotating flows of cells meet at the posterior end, where the streak forms.

subjective.question: Describe digestion in the small intestine.
subjective.answer: Duodenum: When chyme passes from the stomach into the duodenum, its acidity stimulates the release of three secretions: (1) digestive enzymes, (2) pancreatic enzymes, and (3) bile. Intestinal enzymes: In the duodenum, digestion of carbohydrates and proteins is completed, and most lipids are digested. The jejunum and ileum absorb the end products of digestion (amino acids, simple sugars, fatty acids, glycerol, nucleotides, water). Absorption of foods: Much of this absorption involves active transport and the sodium-dependent ATPase pump. Sugars and amino acids are absorbed into the capillaries of the villi. Free fatty acids enter the epithelial cells of the villi and recombine with glycerol to form triglycerides. The triglycerides are coated with proteins to form small droplets called chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals of the villi.

subjective.question: What are the functions of the small intestine?
subjective.answer: In the duodenum, digestion of carbohydrates and proteins is completed, and most lipids are digested. The main function of the jejunum is absorption of important nutrients — sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids. The function of the ileum is mainly to absorb vitamin B12, bile salts, and any products of digestion that were not absorbed by the jejunum.

subjective.question: How do freshwater teleosts osmoregulate in fresh water?
subjective.answer: To combat the osmotic gain of water and loss of salts, freshwater fish have very efficient kidneys that excrete water quickly. They also reabsorb salt from their urine before it is ejected to minimize losses, and actively take salt from their environment using special cells in the gills.

subjective.question: Define nutrition and nutrients. What are organic and inorganic nutrients?
subjective.answer: Nutrition includes all of those processes by which an animal takes in, digests, absorbs, stores, and uses food (nutrients) to meet its metabolic needs. A nutrient is a component in foods that an organism uses to survive and grow. Nutrients may be organic or inorganic. Organic nutrients consist of carbohydrates, fats, proteins (or their building blocks, amino acids), and vitamins. Inorganic nutrients are dietary minerals, water, and oxygen.

subjective.question: What are suspension feeders and deposit feeders? Give examples.
subjective.answer: A suspension feeder is an animal that feeds on material (such as plankton) suspended in water, filtering it out as water passes through or over its body; examples include many bivalve molluscs and sponges. Deposit feeders are primarily omnivorous animals that simply swallow large quantities of sediment (mud, soil, sand, organic matter) and digest the usable nutrients from it; examples include earthworms, many polychaetes, and some sea urchins.

subjective.question: Differentiate between ectotherms and endotherms.
subjective.answer: Ectotherms derive most of their body heat from the environment rather than from their own metabolism; most invertebrates, fishes, amphibians, and reptiles are ectotherms, and they tend to move about the environment and find places that minimize heat or cold stress to their bodies. Endotherms obtain their body heat from cellular processes (their own metabolism); most endotherms have bodies insulated by feathers or fur and a relatively large amount of fat, and endothermy allows animals to stabilize their core temperature.

subjective.question: What is hibernation? On what factors does its duration depend?
subjective.answer: Hibernation is a state of inactivity and metabolic depression in endotherms during winter, in which body temperature, heart rate, and metabolic rate drop greatly so the animal survives on stored body fat when food is scarce. Hibernation may last for days, weeks, or months; its duration depends on the species, the ambient temperature, and the time of the year.

subjective.question: How do marine teleost fishes osmoregulate in sea water?
subjective.answer: Marine teleosts constantly lose water osmotically to the surrounding sea water and gain excess salts. To compensate, they drink large quantities of sea water, excrete the excess salt actively through special chloride cells in the gills, and produce only a very small volume of urine through their kidneys to conserve water.

subjective.question: What are chylomicrons and lacteals?
subjective.answer: In the villi of the small intestine, free fatty acids absorbed by the epithelial cells recombine with glycerol to form triglycerides. These triglycerides are coated with proteins to form small droplets called chylomicrons. The chylomicrons enter the lacteals — the lymph capillaries located in the center of each villus — from where the absorbed fats are carried into the lymphatic system.

subjective.question: What is peristalsis? How does it differ from segmentation?
subjective.answer: Peristalsis is the wave-like, coordinated contraction of the muscle layers of the gastrointestinal tract that propels food along the tract from the oral cavity towards the rectum. Segmentation consists of localized contractions of the circular muscles that mix the food material (chyme) with the digestive secretions and bring it into contact with the absorptive mucosa, rather than moving it mainly in one direction.

subjective.question: Why can ruminants digest cellulose while most other mammals cannot?
subjective.answer: Cellulose contains a large amount of energy, but animals generally lack the ability to produce the enzyme cellulase needed to digest cellulose and obtain its energy. The ruminant stomach harbors large numbers of microorganisms that can produce cellulase, so these microbes ferment and digest the cellulose walls of grass and other vegetation for the host, making the herbivorous lifestyle more effective.
